01 / ABOUT THE WRITER
A little about me
I’m Lindsay Morris, a writer and performer based in Richmond, Virginia. My work spans short
fiction, stage plays, sketch, and live storytelling, with a particular interest in complicated
characters, uncomfortable situations, and the strange places where comedy and vulnerability
overlap.
My writing has been published in Intrinsick Magazine and Santa Clara Review, and my work
has been featured in New York, New Orleans, Chicago, and Richmond. I’m currently active at
Coalition Theater in Richmond, following several years of writing, editing, and performing
with theater companies in Chicago and New Orleans.
Publications & highlights
• Published fiction: Intrinsick Magazine and Santa Clara Review.
• Theater work presented at the Athenaeum Theatre and Green House Theater Center in Chicago.
• Original audio storytelling selected for Other World Theater’s Gateways series.
• Live storytelling, theatrical writing, and performance across four cities.

The writing

01 Lucky Boy SPECULATIVE FICTION
A dark, unsettling story about institutional power, enforced obedience, and the people

A retail worker navigates corporate pressure, private humiliation, and an increasingly
fragile sense of control.

A mordantly funny, self-protective narrator confronts grief, addiction, and the limits of

MORRIS · WRITING PORTFOLIO
LINDSAY MORRIS / NARRATIVE WRITING
01 / COMPLETE SHORT FICTION
Lucky Boy
SPECULATIVE THRILLER
Joey can’t stop pissing himself. That squirming, red-haired motherfucker. When I complain,
they give me the heavy chain, shackle me with double-knotted steel cinched tight at my waist.
No stretching my legs over the Atlantic now.
I lay my elbows on the stripped plastic armrests and stare at the mini screen cracked into
dozens of fresh spiderwebs. The plane has clearly been built for luxury, and despite the
guards’ best efforts, it still shows. Some amenities they’d gone out of their way to ruin, like the
inflight movies, others they’d simply locked away. Half a dozen of us can’t look away from a
bottle of Don Julio sealed behind a glass case a few rows ahead.
When we left Fort Sumter, it was still dark. By the time we boarded in Charleston, the sun was
coming up from the east. Hours later it was rising again. I swear we’re flying in circles,
pumping and dumping fuel all over the country, before touching down.
“They’re trying to keep it hush-hush,” Joey says.
“What?”
“I don’t know.”
“What don’t you know?”
“Everything.”
We both laugh. I look down at the dark stain drying between his legs and I feel bad for calling
him out about the whole pissing-his-pants thing. I hadn’t realized how young he was. No way
this rugrat is built for whatever these bastards have in store.
As the hours stretch on, the guards stop bothering to check on us, occasionally tossing packs of
crackers to shut up the worst of the complainers. I tear the plastic open and share a square.
“Thanks—”
Joey stalls, eyes flicking to the redacted lanyard shoved around my neck.
“It’s Matterson,” I say.
MORRIS • WRITING PORTFOLIO / 3
LINDSAY MORRIS / NARRATIVE WRITING
“Thanks, Mr. Matterson.”
I nod and do my best to get comfortable, ignoring the shifting metal on my groin. None of the
seats recline. Someone shoved glue into the little switch by my side. I scratch at it with my nail
for a while, trying to get the thing to give, but eventually I give up, cross my arms over my
chest, and shut my eyes.
A few hours later I wake up shivering. It was hot when we took off, my pits slick and spicy
from the humid Southern air. The guards on the plane are now dressed for much colder
weather, outfitted in well-worn blue camo. Some have stripped off their thick fleeces and
stretched out; others stayed fully dressed, even keeping their ski masks on.
Tap Tap Tap.
I turn my head and clock Joey smiling.
When he realizes I’m not going to ream him out, he goes back to tapping against the glass,
stopping every few seconds to lift his head, looking for one of the guards before starting up
again.
Behind me, someone picks it up. Tap Tap Tap.
“Knock it off,” a guard barks, not even looking up.
But then another prisoner joins in. Then another. Fingers on plastic. Nails on glass. The
rhythm hopping rows, skipping seats, landing wherever it can. Tap Tap Tap.
“One a penny, two a penny,” I mumble.
Half the plane is in on it, tapping on armrests, trays, windows, knees, anything they can get
their hands on, before one of the guards finally stands, kills the lights, and tells us to eat shit
and die.
At least the lights are off.
Hours later when they unshackle us, I feel a flicker of relief, a brief burst of hope. Dumbass.
The doors are open now and we’re lined up like good little inmates, freezing our asses off
while we wait for our voluntary rehabilitation to begin. Snow comes down heavy, big freaking
flakes swallowing the ground, making it impossible to get decent leverage as they march us
forward, left, right, left, knee to chest, ass to groin, slipping and sliding through the worst of it.
I already miss the warm shackles of the plane’s fuselage interior.
MORRIS • WRITING PORTFOLIO / 4
LINDSAY MORRIS / NARRATIVE WRITING
Joey is whimpering, cradling his right palm. A piece of skin froze to the metal walkway as we
exited the plane and he had to rip it off to keep the line moving.
“My mom didn’t say it was gonna be cold,” he says miserably, a few stray tears already icing
beneath his eyes.
I stick my tongue out, guiding it in little waves and divots as I attempt to catch a falling
snowflake. A six-sided beauty lands on the tip of my glossa; it tastes like nothing.
Visibility is awful, but even still, it doesn’t take more than a second to look around and know
we’ve fucked off to the absolute ass end of the United States, if we’re even still in the US. No
laws, no justice. A perfect black hole caked in pretty white snow. I don’t have a clue where we
are, but it doesn’t matter. North Dakota or Jupiter, either way, Lady Liberty, that green-eyed
bitch wasn't looking.
Most of us do our best to hustle forward until the line comes into view. Other planes must
have landed before us. Dozens of inmates stretch out as far as the eye can see, the line
bending around a small wooden shack where a few guards stand clustered together, cigarette
smoke misting above their heads, before looping back toward the building.
Past them, against the bone-white mountains, stands a hulking mass of cold steel and
industry, its bottom half swallowed by rock and snow. Above it, an oblong metal cap bulges
with a single long window wrapping around it like a visor. At its base is a fat gray door; in the
distance, I can spot a series of red and green lights winking on and off as other inmates step
off the line and dart inside.
“I gotta say, zero points for creativity.” The whole thing screams Secret Government Facility.
“Is that where they're gonna do it?” Joey asks, not taking his eyes off of the metal dome.
“Yep. That's where they’re gonna do it.”
Joey finally shuts up, wide eyes flicking up and down before shoving his injured hand into his
jumpsuit, cradling it to his chest. We don’t speak for the next little while, inching along minute
by minute, all of us shivering, eyeing the guards' cheap wool jackets and padded camo pants
with frigid envy. Is there anything worse than bureaucracy in the face of the American death
star?
The security guard to my right prowls back and forth, warning us to stay in line. He smokes
Pall Malls at a healthy pace, giving us the stink eye after each used butt. It isn’t like anyone is
stupid enough to run. We can hardly walk in this shit. If anything, I want to be “rehabilitated”
faster if it means getting out of this cold. How quickly resistance dies in zero degree weather.
MORRIS • WRITING PORTFOLIO / 5
LINDSAY MORRIS / NARRATIVE WRITING
Behind me, one of the less ambitious delinquents is complaining; he griped nonstop on the
flight over. I turn to look at the guy. He has close-cropped, freshly buzzed bleach blond hair.
His eyebrows are thick black stumps connected by a few stubborn wisps down the middle.
“It’s not fair. I shouldn’t even be here!” he yells over the wind. He kicks at the snow, sending
an icy spray back into his own face. “All I did was post a few memes. I wasn’t even the OP.”
“Did you tell them that?” Joey asks, perking up for the first time since we got off the plane.
“Yeah. But those phony cops wouldn’t hear it,” he says. “Since when are memes treason
anyway?”
He looks at Joey. “You online a lot?”
Joey shakes his head.
“Figures. I’m kind of famous,” he says. “When we get back, look me up. ZinnWazRight69. I’m
the original Milkshake Kid.”
We both shook our heads.
“Come on. You know the one.”
He makes a face, shoves a fist to his chin, arranges his mouth like he’s about to shit.
When we don’t say anything, he keeps going. “They said they already nailed some X user for
it. But it was me. I’m telling you.”
He snorts. “There’s records and shit. No way they wipe me completely.”
Joey nods and the guy gives him a rough couple of knuckles to the head. They scuffle a bit,
Joey losing his footing, going down twice in the snow before they both come away smiling.
ZinnWazRight69 is a full-on jackass, insufferable in a way that would’ve made us friends if
we’d met a dozen years ago.
I look around at the lot of us. All men. All assholes. And if you ask me, not one of them
deserves whatever’s coming.
But no one asks me.
A few minutes later one of the guys drops down behind us. I see two men propping him up
between them, slapping his cheeks, shouting into his face, trying to keep him moving. The line
doesn’t stop.
MORRIS • WRITING PORTFOLIO / 6
LINDSAY MORRIS / NARRATIVE WRITING
The snow has soaked through our prison shoes, cold seeping up from the soles, numbing
ankles, deadening toes. Every step feels heavier than the last. The cold isn’t just on us
anymore. It’s inside us, burrowed deep until we’re all shaking and shivering.
Joey starts coughing, choking on phlegm and snot, and ZinnWazRight69’s got an arm around
him, giving his back a few hard slaps. “Come on. Get it out.”
“Hey,” he calls out to one of the passing guards. “Can’t you see the kid’s freezing to death?”
The guard doesn’t look back. Just keeps moving.
ZinnWazRight69 watches him go, jaw tight. He snorts, louder now. “Come on, man. I’m
freezing my nuts off.”
He grabs his whole package and sort of wangles himself around, gaining a little height in the
process. Even in this temperature I catch the faint outline of flesh beneath his thin prison
jumpsuit. A few of us laugh. Not because it’s funny, but because it’s better than not laughing.
“You know who I am?” he calls after the guard. “I’m the fucking Milkshake Kid.” He grins.
“You hear me, you fascist fuck?”
The guard, a real thick son of a bitch, yanks him out of line.
“Finally, man,” ZinnWazRight69 says, still smirking. “I’ve been waiting all day.”
The guard throws an elbow into his face.
“Watch his mouth,” another guard says, coming to help as they pull him toward the shack.
“Yeah. Watch my mouth.”
He manages to yank a hand free, spreads a sloppy V with his fingers, sticks his tongue out and
rolls it back and forth in fleshy waves.
The other guard gets in a punch to the kidney, and you can hear the breath rattle out of him as
they drag him toward the shack, slamming the door shut behind him.
“He’s gonna come back, isn't he?” Joey asks.
“Course he is.” Not a shot.
MORRIS • WRITING PORTFOLIO / 7
LINDSAY MORRIS / NARRATIVE WRITING
Another guard wearing a ski mask and visor, bulging and faceless, comes by a minute later
handing out juice boxes. He hands me a heavy brick, Pineapple Sunshine, the plastic frozen
solid.
Bastard.
I grip it in my hands, flex it between my blue-tipped fingers before shoving it in my pocket.
Joey tries to get his open, but with only one working hand, he’s struggling. His lip snags on the
corner where he’s trying to use his teeth and bright red blood blooms fresh on his lip.
My paternal instincts kick in because I grab his juice box instead, wrench the frozen corner
loose, and press it into his hand. “Wipe your mouth,” I tell him.
He does, then licks at the edge of the juice, getting a little Sunshine into him, his eyes going
wide as the sugar hits. His tongue sticks on contact, the pink stretching as he pulls back. He
goes in again, breathing hard on the surface to coax a little warmth before trying once more.
We’re getting closer now, playing red light, green light. The snow is no longer big and fluffy;
it’s turned mean, frozen pellets buzzing past my ear. A constant heavy static rattling all
around me.
“Looks like I’m almost up,” I yell to Joey.
“Don’t leave me,” he says.
“You’ll be fine. Just a few harmless cuts, a little snip-snip, and we’ll be back on that plane
before you know it.” I try to mimic a pair of scissors but my fingers are too numb to make it
look right.
I turn to go through but he clings to my arm. I grab his hand, give it a squeeze, then lift it off.
“Try not to piss yourself again, kid,” I say, and rush through as soon as the door slides open.
My hands fly up on instinct, palms pressed hard over my eyes, my whole body convulsing in
sharp, involuntary twitches as the heat of the room thaws me out like frostbitten chicken.
It takes a moment for me to get what's what, but eventually I get myself going. The room is
bright, overly large, a mix of metal and blue tile set in dark gray grout covering the walls. The
ceiling is gridded with long fluorescent panels sunk into white acoustic plates, muting a faint
hum I can feel low in my gut.
“Jamie Matterson?” A middle-aged woman with a fat ass asks.
MORRIS • WRITING PORTFOLIO / 8
LINDSAY MORRIS / NARRATIVE WRITING
I nod. She gestures me forward, already moving behind her boat-like metal desk. I step up to
the desk, my feet landing on a red X taped to the floor.
“Welcome to the Prosthetic Occlusion Compliance Clinic, Jamie," she says sweetly.
Reperfusion tears through my arms and legs, sharp needles bursting into cherry red flames as
circulation staggers back. I shift my weight, hunting for a scrap of relief. My right leg bounces
without permission, jittering up and down as the cold drains out of it.
“Please stand still while our computer finishes its scans.”
“And if I don’t?” I say. “If I tell you to go fuck yourself after keeping me out in the cold all
night?”
The woman behind the desk smiles a little wider. “If you don’t do what you’re told, Jamie, I’ll
have one of the guards come in, break your legs, and hold you up until I’m finished with you.”
I give her a little fuck you salute and stand still.
“No defects, abnormalities, or signs of cancerous rot,” she says. “Aren’t you the healthy boy.”
“You’re coming on a bit strong, aren't you?” I say, forcing a wink. “What time do you get off
tonight?”
She ignores me and puts a fresh tablet on the desk.
“Sign here.” The tablet lights up, revealing bright white disclaimers in bold black lettering.
There are hundreds of pages in the terms and conditions for me to read. I try to scan the first
few paragraphs but after a minute I give up, scroll to the bottom, and sign.
I know a bullshit deal when I see one, but what are you gonna do? They had me dead to rights.
“Come on now,” I say. “I’m a great lay. Ask my ex, Kiko. She said the only thing wrong with me
was my shitty personality. Not a word against my pecker, I swear.”
“We also need verbal consent. Please turn your head towards the camera,” she says icily, that
pretty little smile turning sour.
“Which one?” I look around; the place is covered with them. Mounted in the corners of the
ceiling, bolted onto scanning machines. Hell, there was even one dangling from the chest of
fat ass right above her security clearance badge.
“Pick one,” she says, annoyed.
MORRIS • WRITING PORTFOLIO / 9
LINDSAY MORRIS / NARRATIVE WRITING
I choose tits.
“Do you agree to allow us to remove your molars, incisors, front teeth, back teeth, gum line,
and jaw bone if necessary?”
I sort of wish I hadn't skipped those pages.
I nod, then remember myself. “Yes. Only if necessary? Right?”
“Next,” the woman calls, and I am already being corralled down a long, millennium gray
hallway by one of the nameless camo boys. Now that the hour is actually upon me, I am no
longer so keen on the deal after all.
My hand slips into my pocket and finds the juice box, still half frozen, slick with condensation.
My fingers tighten around Pineapple Sunshine.
“Hey,” I say, turning just enough to catch the guard’s attention.
I bring the juice box down hard. The carton connects with the top of his skull. The sound is
ugly and wet, like striking rain-soaked wood. He stumbles forward and I am grateful for the
anonymity of the ski mask. I do not want to know his face.
I turn and run, barreling down the hall. Locked doors on all sides. I grab handles at random
and I can smell my fear sweating through my jumpsuit. This was a really fucking dumb idea.
It occurs to me, too late, that the guard might have had keys. Or a security badge or a fucking
phone.
I double back and find him no longer crumpled on the floor, but on his hands and knees,
already pushing himself upright.
“You motherfucker,” he says, rubbing the top of his head.
I drop to the floor and reach for his pockets as he struggles to stand. It's awkward, all elbows
and knees, the two of us tangled on the floor like idiots.
“I don’t have anything,” he snaps, shoving me off. “They don’t give us shit.”
We end up sitting there for a second, backs against the wall, knees up. He keeps rubbing his
head and I keep breathing too fast.
“You got two choices,” he says finally. “Go where I tell you, or get us both in trouble and go
right down the fucking mountain.”
MORRIS • WRITING PORTFOLIO / 10
LINDSAY MORRIS / NARRATIVE WRITING
“I’ll take the first one.”
He gets to his feet, hauls me up by the arm, walks ten feet, gut punches me, and shoves me
through the nearest open door.
“Jesus,” I hear him mutter as it slams shut. “I hate this job.”
It doesn't look like any dentist’s office I’ve ever seen. I thought the equipment would be silver.
I thought it would smell like fluoride and root beer. Goddamnit. I even let myself hope for
those little lollipops they hand you after they floss your teeth.
Everything is wrong. From the uniformed grey walls to the chair with its thick metal
restraints and the sour smell of ammonia permeating the air.
Fifteen minutes of freedom. Those first sweet steps of patriotic duty, and this is the reward.
It hardly seems fair.
But nothing has been fair in a long time. Not work. Not life, and certainly not the government.
I don’t even know what the hell came over me. One minute I’m rushing home to make dinner,
trying to decide if it’s worth texting Kiko again or if I should just throw in the towel, and the
next thing I know some Steely Dan motherfucker hands me a sign and I’m chanting with all
the rest of them, fist high above me.
All around me were sweaty faces, sun-blotched skin, bony arms, pit-stained shirts. Bodies
pressed close as we marched and sang, spitting out the furious taste of a system built against
us. I was. We were. In sync.
I didn't even realize until we were half way down First Ave that I was marching for anybody
other than myself. That maybe it wasn't just me that was sick of getting reamed out by my
manager and her manager and all the managers before her.
It wasn't my fault someone hoisted me on their shoulders. It wasn't my fault that it felt so
damn good. Fifteen minutes later a policeman had a boot on my neck and he didn't want to
hear it wasn't my fault. I was arrested for the first time in my life. Never in my wildest fucking
nightmares did I think it could happen to someone like me. What can I say? I thought I was
immune. Exempt. Free and clear from any and all police brutality. They charged me with so
many crimes it was separated by a second page break.
I have never felt such fear. Such cold, naked terror.
MORRIS • WRITING PORTFOLIO / 11
LINDSAY MORRIS / NARRATIVE WRITING
Then, beneath the words fifteen to life and Treason with a capital T, was the little check box
that opted out of a trial in exchange for “experimental rehabilitation.”
It wasn't fair, and somehow it still surprised me I ever thought it would be.
I lie back in the chair. Why fight it?
The dentist comes in wearing a gray mask and matching scrubs. His eyes are bright blue.
Cerulean, my mother would have said. She loved colors and hated politics.
She doesn’t know I’m here. Never even got the chance to break her heart. One phone call my
ass.
“Do you guys ever think of choosing another color? All this metal on metal shit is really
ahhhh.”
It hits my sinuses before I can process what happened, the spray, the mace, whatever the fuck
it is the bastard just held up to my face, immediately gets absorbed by all those microscopic
blood vessels in my mouth.
I gag a few times. I feel my whole body convulse, swallowing itself bit by bit until eventually
I’m spit out again, a jellied wet mass.
“How about a little warning next time?” I sit up, wipe my face clumsily, my jaw already going
numb.
“There won't be a next time, Jamie. Please lay down,” He pushes my head until it hits the
headrest.
The lights dim. “Was that real, or was I just imagining it?”
He winks at me, then activates the restraints on the table. My arms become immobile. Not that
I could move them anyway.
“Relax, Jamie.”
But I can’t relax. And I hate that he keeps using my name. We aren’t buddies, he isn’t someone
I want with their fingers all up in my mucosa.
The doctor sticks something in my mouth. My tongue gets a taste of copper, bright fresh
pennies dripping down my throat as my lips stretch wider and wider. He sticks a gloved finger
inside me, tickling my uvula, and I can feel spittle beginning to flow down my chin.
MORRIS • WRITING PORTFOLIO / 12
LINDSAY MORRIS / NARRATIVE WRITING
“I want to goh fhomme,” I say. I can't help it.
The doctor nods but continues to work on my mouth.
“You’ve got a beautiful set of incisors.” I hear the clink clink as he taps them with professional
admiration. Feel the vibration in my collarbone.
“Some of these boys who come in. No standards. Mouth full of cavities.”
He wrinkles his nose. “But every once in a while I get a beautiful set to work with. Just the
other day I had a boy on my table with the most handsome molars. Broke my heart, ripping
them out.”
He turns and uncovers a tray. I get a glimpse of dark titanium wires, thick copper filament,
tiny Phillips-head screws. Nasty pieces of hardware laid out in rows. None of it gleaming.
None of it new and none of it looks like it belongs anywhere near my mouth.
“You have no idea what a lucky boy you are,” he says, grabbing a pair of pliers off the tray.
“This is far more humane than what we used to do.”
He shoves the pliers into the back of my mouth. I feel a sharp pressure, then an impossible
pull, something tears. He sticks his hand back into my mouth and a moment later comes away
satisfied, a nerve, dangling and wiggly like a worm, between his fingers.
“Lots of problems with those earlier iterations,” He continues, wiping his bloody glove on a
towel beside him. “People trying to claw out their new implants. I imagine the pain was
excruciating, not sure how some of them managed it. But don’t worry, we learned the hard
way lithium batteries and flesh just don’t mix.”
There is a rapid escalation of sound, spinning metal grinding against teeth. I can feel the noise
in my skull.
“Now for the fun part.”
I am terrified and I don't believe for a minute all the little lies the drugs are telling my nerve
endings.
“Don’t worry. We’ll have you fixed up in a jiffy, minimal scarring. Nobody will notice a thing.
And the best part? Your worst impulses, those nasty things you said or did to get yourself here,
won’t ever be a problem again.
“Fwuk You!” bloody spit lands all over his grey scrubs. There is so much red everywhere.
MORRIS • WRITING PORTFOLIO / 13
LINDSAY MORRIS / NARRATIVE WRITING
“Merciful, really.” He says dabbing at his chest with the towel.
My eyes flicker back to the doctor’s baby blues.
He pulls a light down from above my head and I try to turn away, but it shines so bright I
think I’ve gone blind, and without ever choosing it, the darkness carries me away.
I wake up in stages. My head is pounding and my ass aches from whatever shitty seat I’ve
been shoved into.
My eyes open to a large sliver of daylight. I’m in a window seat, back on the plane. From what
I can tell, Good Old America is staring back at me through the glass to my right. Whether it’s
the same one I left, I couldn’t say.
All around me are wrapped faces. Bandaged jaws. Shirts soaked with drool, laps heavy with
bloody cotton. I feel something wet and warm slide down the back of my neck.
My hand moves clumsily to my head and come away holding a lukewarm bag I assume was
once filled with ice.
I reach up to touch my face and it feels numb. My fingers trace the swollen parts of my jaw.
“Fwhat dith theYhh do?” I ask the guy to the left of me.
His eyes seemed cloudy and panicked under a shock of distinctive copper eyebrows. All the
more gruesome against a crown of white gauze.
“Jowey. Arw You Awhight?”
His jaw is moving bizarrely, opening and closing disjointedly, nothing but a waspy rattle
coming out as the terror in his eyes grows.
“Okay, patriots. Listen up.” I crane my neck and lift up in my seat.
The guard at the front of the plane has his mask off. He looks early fifties. His army wannabe
crew cut can’t disguise the balding at his temples. His posture is unnatural, a cheap imitation
of a German shepherd held at attention.
“I said wake up.”
He kicks the back of a seat with his heavy black boots. The man in it lurches forward, still
foggy.
MORRIS • WRITING PORTFOLIO / 14
LINDSAY MORRIS / NARRATIVE WRITING
“You’ve all been rehabilitated at the great expense of the United States of America.”
He claps once, then walks slowly down the aisle, his hand dragging over the gauze of a few
shaved heads.
“Thanks to science, or engineering, or whatever the hell it was, Lady Liberty will be shining
her satellite on you, twenty-four-seven. That means no more nasty words out of those
